intro: An n-step target combines several observed rewards with a later value prediction. A terminal event or rollout boundary can shorten that lookahead.
task: Construct a target for every starting transition. Keep track of how many rewards were consumed so the bootstrap receives the correct discount power.
requirements: rewards and terminated have length T in 1..255, values has length T+1, and terminated contains numeric zero/one. discount is in [0,1], and steps is an integer in [1,256].

Starting at each t, accumulate up to steps rewards with powers discount**0, discount**1, etc. Stop after including a terminal transition’s reward. Otherwise add discount**k*values[t+k], where k rewards were consumed.
At a nonterminal rollout cutoff use the final supplied value, even when fewer than steps rewards remain. Never cross a terminal into the next episode. Return a NumPy vector of length T.

Use real finite numeric inputs of magnitude at most 1e30, excluding boolean parameters. Vectors have 1..256 entries and each matrix axis has length 1..256 unless a stricter bound is stated. Leave caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Count consumed transitions
hints.body: The bootstrap exponent equals the number of rewards included, not the requested horizon when the rollout is shorter.

hints.title: Include the terminal reward
hints.body: Stopping an episode removes the later value, not the reward observed on its last transition.

explanation: At a one-step horizon the target uses one reward and the next value. With a horizon spanning the rollout, it equals the bootstrapped return recurrence.
The later value trades an observed long-term sum for a prediction. This lesson isolates horizon and boundary mechanics rather than asserting a universally best horizon.
